  MOTT ENERGY, LLC LONG MOTT GENERATING STATION CONSTRUCTION PERMIT
                               APPLICATION

      Applicant:                 Long Mott Energy, LLC

1.0      BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE

By letter dated March 31, 2025 (Agencywide Documents Access and Management System
(ADAMS) Package Accession No. ML25090A057), Long Mott Energy, LLC (LME) submitted a
construction permit (CP) application for a reactor facility pursuant to Title 10 of the Code of
Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization
Facilities,” to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for review. The facility, referred to
as Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS), would be constructed in Calhoun County, Texas. By
letter dated May 12, 2025, the NRC staff (the staff) accepted the CP application for detailed
review (ML25115A247). The NRC staff conducted a detailed review of the LMGS CP application
and engaged in regulatory audits as described below to assist the NRC staff in its review.
Revision 1 of the CP application was submitted by LME on September 18, 2026.

The general audit plan was issued on June 5, 2025 (ML25128A332), the probabilistic risk
assessment (PRA) audit plan was issued on June 11, 2025 (ML25156A350), and the Chapter
2 and structures audit plan was issued on June 25, 2025 (ML26048A641). The purpose of
these audits was to enable the staff to gain understanding, confirm information, and/or identify
information that would require docketing to support the basis for the staff’s regulatory decision.

2.0      AUDIT REGULATORY BASES

The basis for the audits are the regulations in 10 CFR pertinent to the NRC staff’s review of the
CP application, including 10 CFR 50.34, “Contents of applications; technical information,”
10 CFR 50.35, “Issuance of construction permits,” 10 CFR 100.20, “Factors to be considered
when evaluating sites,” 10 CFR 100.21, “Non-seismic site criteria,” 10 CFR 100.23, “Geologic
and seismic siting criteria,” and Appendix S to Part 50, “Earthquake Engineering Criteria for
Nuclear Power Plants.”

4.0    AUDIT PROCESS

The audits were primarily conducted remotely via the LME electronic reading room (eRR)
and video teleconferences. In addition, in-person meetings were held at NRC
Headquarters in Rockville, Maryland and X-Energy Offices in Rockville, Maryland. The
general audit, PRA audit, and chapter 2 and structures audit began on Jun 5, 2025,
June 11, 2025, and June 25, 2025, respectively, and all audits ended on October 23, 2026.
The NRC staff conducted the audits in accordance with the Office of Nuclear Reactor
Regulation (NRR) Office Instruction LIC-111, Revision 1, “Regulatory Audits,”
(ML19226A274).

The NRC staff’s audits focused on supporting documents and information associated with the
topics identified in the audit plans. Through the NRC external SharePoint site, the NRC staff
transmitted audit questions, including document requests, to clearly identify the information
needed to support the NRC staff’s review. Enclosure 5 of this audit report contains a list of
documents that were placed in the eRR by LME. The NRC staff audited information provided
by LME in the eRR and held discussions with LME staff to understand the LMGS preliminary
design and resolve questions. In many cases, LME updated the preliminary safety analysis
report (PSAR) to resolve items discussed in the audit.
                                                    4


5.0       AUDIT ACTIVITIES AND RESULTS

Some of the important topic areas that were discussed during the audit include:

      •   Principal Design Criteria (PDCs)

          The NRC staff discussed the limited PDC LBE scope (i.e., AOO for CDC, DBE/DBA for
          RFDC) with LME. Through this discussion it was understood that the SSC performance
          was evaluated for all LBEs credited with performing prevention and mitigation safety
          functions, and that evaluation feeds back into the design through SSC-specific design
          requirements, reliability and capability targets, and special treatments. Revisions to
          PSAR sections 6.3 and 7.2 summarized this process.

          Additionally, audit discussions resulted in revisions to PSAR chapters 6 and 7 to support
          NRC staff conclusions that the preliminary design of SSCs is consistent with the relevant
          PDCs.

      •   Research and Development (R&D)

          The NRC staff discussed R&D program scope with LME. Through this discussion it was
          understood that aspects of the materials qualification program, discussed in PSAR
          chapter 3.8, that are associated with metallic safety related SSCs are in scope of the
          R&D program. In addition, items associated with the graphite topical report, discussed in
          PSAR table 1.4-14, and fuel qualification, discussed in PSAR table 6.4.2-1, are in scope.
          Results of this discussion are captured in PSAR chapter 13.

      •   Defuel Chute

          The NRC staff discussed the defuel chute with LME. The defuel chute performs an
          important function in providing structural support to the pebbles within the core as the
          fuel pebbles transition from the high temperature core environment to the lower
          temperature fuel handling system. The discussion included the pressure vessel that
          surrounds and supports the defuel chute, the vessel that receives the fuel as it exits the
          defuel chute, and the equipment that controls the rate of fuel movement. The NRC staff
          sought an understanding of how the environmental conditions would be evaluated and
          how potential accident conditions had been considered.

          Through this discussion and review of supporting preliminary thermal analyses, the NRC
          staff gained an understanding of the current development of the defuel chute design and
          its importance to safety. The applicant included applicable safety-related defuel chute
          metallic materials in the R&D program and further explained plans for additional analysis
          related to evaluation of the following: accident conditions identified through probabilistic
          approaches; potential consequences of failure; and thermal conditions, including
          changes in the decay of fuel entering the defuel chute. This engagement resulted in
          revisions to PSAR sections 6.4.5, 6.4.8, and 7.3.6.

      •   Hydrology

          The NRC staff conducted a series of audit discussions to develop an understanding of
          the process, data, and methodologies used to evaluate plausible flood causing
                                              5


    mechanisms at the LMGS site, groundwater flow characteristics and levels, and the
    postulated accidental radioactive liquid effluents transport analysis. The discussions also
    included considerations of flood mitigation mechanisms to provide reasonable assurance
    about the protection of SSCs important to safety. These engagements resulted in
    revisions to PSAR section 2.4.

•   Dispersion Factors

    The NRC staff conducted a series of audit discussions to develop an understanding of
    the inputs, assumptions, and methodologies used to evaluate the atmospheric
    dispersion for the LMGS site. The discussions included the reasons for any departures
    from the analysis outlined in the atmospheric dispersion and dose consequences
    methodology topical report. The discussions also included details of the site-specific
    analysis that will be included in a future operating license application to verify that
    conservative dispersion values are used in analyses for the LMGS site. These
    engagements resulted in revisions to PSAR sections 2.3.4, 2.3.5, and 11.4.

•   Structural Engineering

    The NRC staff discussed with LME differences between the safety classification for
    safety significant SSCs and the safety classification of structures in their load path that
    provide essential support. LME revised the safety classification of certain structures and
    updated its seismic categorization approach, including enhanced seismic treatment for
    NSRST structures supporting SR SSCs, to ensure that structures providing load path
    support achieve performance levels consistent with the SSCs they are supporting.

    Additionally, the NRC staff reviewed and discussed supporting structural/seismic design
    and analysis information including demand and capacity determinations, analysis,
    design, and construction techniques for precast concrete systems. The NRC staff also
    reviewed analysis techniques for developing seismic design inputs, including verification
    of earthquake time histories against design response spectra enveloping criteria and
    target power spectral density function, and the development of the design response
    spectra and associated site class for non-safety-related SSCs. The NRC staff gained an
    understanding of the structural/seismic analysis and design information described in the
    PSAR. These discussions resulted in updates to PSAR sections and tables including,
    section 3.7.6.1, table 3.7-3, section 6.4.1.2.1, and table 6.4.1-2.

•   Structural Integrity of Metallic Materials

    The NRC staff discussed the structural integrity evaluation method for metallic
    components with LME and requested supporting information on the codes and
    standards selection and supplementation, as well as environmental compatibility
    assessment. These engagements resulted in revisions to PSAR section 3.8.

•   Structural Materials

    The NRC staff discussed the SR and NSRST structural materials with LME and
    requested supporting information on the material, environment, selected codes and
    standards, code supplementation, and special treatments. These engagements resulted
    in revisions to PSAR Chapters 6 and 7.
                                             6



•   Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ)

    The NRC staff discussed LME’s implementation of the plume exposure pathway (PEP)
    emergency planning zone sizing (EPZ) methodology. The audit focused on LME’s
    implementation of the methodology used to establish the site-specific PEP EPZ size for
    the LMGS site. These engagements resulted in revisions to Part VI-A of LME’s CP
    application (X-energy, LLC, “Xe-100 Technical Report, Preliminary Plume Exposure
    Pathway Emergency Planning Zone Analysis,” Revision 4).

•   Mechanistic Source Term (MST)

    The NRC staff discussed multiple aspects of the MST, including pebble inventory,
    steady-state inventories, accident source terms, atmospheric dispersion, and
    temperature and thermal hydraulics. The outcome of the audit discussions allowed the
    NRC staff to understand the use of the XSTERM computer code to develop MSTs for
    use in consequence analysis.

•   Inherent Reactivity Feedback

    The NRC staff discussed inherent reactivity feedback with LME. Inherent reactivity is
    one of the two independent means of controlling reactivity for Xe-100 design. As
    described in the PSAR, the second means to meet diversity and independence from
    inherent reactivity feedback, is provided by the control rods and the design is covered
    under PDC-RFDC 26 and PDC-CDC 26. The scope and intent of MHTGR-DC 26 of RG
    1.232 is collectively addressed by PDC 11 and PDC 26 for the Xe-100 design.

    During audit, the NRC staff discussed with LME that the language of PDC-CDC 26 in the
    CP application was not clear and that the words independent and diverse from the
    required functional design criteria seemed to be pointing to PDC-RFDC 26. Based on
    the audit discussions, LME updated PDC-CDC 26 to clarify its applicability as one of the
    two independent and diverse means to control reactivity, i.e., moveable poisons, and
    clarified that independence and diversity discussed in PDC-CDC 26 is from inherent
    reactivity discussed in PDC-RFDC 11. With the change, the scope and intent of
    MHTGR-DC 26, as applicable to Xe-100, is collectively addressed by PDC 11 and PDC
    26.

    In addition to the PDC aspects of inherent reactivity feedback, the NRC staff discussed
    with LME the challenges of using inherent reactivity feedback as a shutdown
    mechanism, which requires higher temperatures to be effective and could be seen as
    conflicting with the fundamental safety function of controlling heat removal. Discussions
    centered around the transient analysis demonstrating that fuel temperature limits are not
    exceeded, with consideration for the full range of initial conditions. LME added
    commitments related to the transient analysis in PSAR section 3.1.7 based on these
    audit discussions.

•   Spent Fuel Storage

    The NRC staff discussed spent fuel storage with respect to cooling and reactivity control
    functions with LME. The NRC staff found that these functions relied heavily on the
                                             7


    control of fuel storage geometry provided by the pebble storage canisters and the
    storage racks supporting the canisters within the storage building. This discussion
    resulted in identification of applicable PDCs and the application of additional special
    treatments to the canisters and storage racks to ensure geometry is maintained and to
    ensure excessive challenges to the contained fuel pebbles are prevented, which are
    described in PSAR sections 3.7 and 7.3.1.3.

•   Reactor Cavity Cooling System (RCCS)

    The NRC staff discussed LME’s plans to address design aspects for the RCCS and to
    complete the development of the RCCS evaluation model. The audit discussion focused
    on the planned integral effects testing program, scaling methodology, and evaluation of
    the applicability of the RCCS model. These engagements resulted in revisions to PSAR
    section 6.4.11.

•   Reliability and Integrity Management (RIM)

    The NRC staff discussed LME’s reliability and integrity (RIM) program, focusing on the
    areas of program scope and degradation mechanism assessments. These engagements
    resulted in revisions to PSAR section 8.2.

•   Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA)

    The NRC staff discussed LME’s development and use of PRA to develop the preliminary
    LMGS licensing basis following the licensing modernization project (LMP) approach and
    application of specific risk insights to the LMGS design. The NRC staff also discussed
    LME’s application of the technical elements in the American Society of Mechanical
    Engineers (ASME) and American Nuclear Society (ANS) RA-S-1.4-2021 non-light water
    reactor PRA standard, the application of appendix A of RG 1.253, and the results of the
    LME self-assessment to assess whether the PRA in use at the CP stage was developed
    using generally accepted methods and reflects an appropriate level of technical rigor to
    support the LMP-related activities.

•   Licensing Modernization Project (LMP) Implementation

    The NRC staff discussed LME’s implementation of the LMP methodology. The audit
    focused on LME’s implementation of licensing basis event (LBE) categorization and
    safety classification of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) and confirming
    consistency with NEI 18-04 and the clarifications in RG 1.233 in these areas. Some
    inconsistencies between LMP and LME’s implementation of LMP were identified through
    the audit discussions. LME made updates to their LMP implementing processes and
    PSAR sections 3.2 and 5.1 based on these audit discussions. The NRC staff also issued
    RCI-1, which LME responded to with confirmation of process changes and preliminary
    results.

•   Fuel and Transition from Non-Fueled to Steady-State Core

    The NRC staff discussed with LME the various pebble types used in the Xe-100 reactor
    design, including startup fuel-free pebbles, low-enriched uranium pebbles, and high-
    assay low-enriched uranium pebbles and the process LME plans to use to transition
                                                8


        from SFFPs to the steady-state core which contains HUPs at various stages of burnup.
        The discussion included aspects such as methods for loading pebbles and transitioning
        between pebble types, the potential placement of the startup source or sources relative
        to the neutron flux detectors, and the points at which LME plans to perform
        measurements of the inherent reactivity feedback, shutdown margin, and other key core
        physics parameters to ensure they are within the scope of their safety analysis. LME
        updated sections 1.1.4.1, 3.1.6, and 6.4.2 of the PSAR based on these audit
        discussions.
